title: As flu hospitalizations spike, Maryland surges $164 million to help overburdened hospitals cope
summary: More than 4,000 Marylanders have been hospitalized with the flu this season, 1,000 with RSV and hundreds more with COVID-19 -- putting a strain on hospitals that state officials hope to ease by releasing $164 million in "surge funding."
content:
By John Domen

It’s been a tough flu season for Marylanders, with more than 4,000 people hospitalized with the flu so far this year, another 1,000 with RSV and hundreds more hospitalized with COVID-19, according to the latest state data.

All of those cases have put a strain on the state’s hospitals, which is why state officials on Thursday announced the release of $164 million in “surge funding” to help hospitals cope with the spike in cases and care for the influx of patients.

“This funding will make sure that hospitals have support to be able to cover the costs of additional staff,” Gov. Wes Moore (D) said. “It will make sure that hospitals have the ability to keep beds open and available.”

The funding comes from the Health Services Cost Review Commission, a state agency that oversees hospital rate-setting in Maryland. Last summer, the commission approved the reauthorization of the surge fund that will be tapped for the hospital payments announced Thursday.

A statement from the governor’s office said the surge funding aims to help hospitals meet the increased staffing and other operational costs that come with the sudden spike in cases. Awards will be divided between 25 hospitals in the state and will range from $49,000 to $32.8 million.

‘Severe’ flu surge may be dropping, but not before putting 4,000 in the hospital, killing 14

Nat Richardson is president and CEO of the University of Maryland Capital Region Health in Largo where Thursday’s event was held. He said his organization plans and budgets for increased needs at this time of year brought on by illnesses such as the flu, but the level of need this year has been overwhelming.

“When you think about a 30% surge in hospitals — that surge, we can’t just go in a closet and pick up a bunch of team members and say, ‘Come help with the surge,’” Richardson said. “We’re typically reaching out to agencies … to bring in additional resources. And those are dollars that we plan for, for the most part, but not at a 30% surge.”

Maryland Health Secretary Dr. Meena Seshamani said the level of respiratory illnesses remains high even after a recent spike in hospitalizations. As of last week, according to the governor’s office, the state had recorded 4,087 flu hospitalizations this season, 976 hospitalizations for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and 569 for COVID-19.

“We are still high,” Seshamani said at the Largo event. “Even when a spike starts to come down, there can be another spike, because people start to relax and say, ‘OK, we’re through that hump,’ and maybe hand washing, other things kind of fall back a little bit.”

She and other state leaders also kept hammering home the point that vaccines of all kinds, but especially flu and COVID-19 shots, are safe and effective. Officials have said even if the vaccines don’t stop someone from getting sick, they reduce the impact the virus has on them.

“The confusion stops here,” Seshamani said. “It is worth it. Vaccines are one of the most powerful tools in our toolbox to keep ourselves healthy. They continue to be the most effective way to protect ourselves and our families against severe illness, and that includes the strains of flu that are circulating now.”
